# Paired centroid tails and independent symmetric additive noise

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): complete auxiliary theorem. The proof uses the standard one-constraint localization theorem of Fradelizi–Guédon, with its precise parameter and semicontinuity conditions recorded below. The scalar inequalities after localization are proved here. This is not a proof of the mixed-integer conjecture.

Write \(\gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d\) for integers \(d\ge1\).

## 1. The paired-tail theorem

Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, let \(g\) be its ordinary volume centroid, and let \(u\ne0\). Put

\[
 F_u(s)=\frac{|K\cap\{x:u\cdot(x-g)\ge s\}|}{|K|}.
\]

Then, for every \(s\ge0\),

\[
                 F_u(s)+F_u(-s)\ge2\gamma_d.                 \tag{1}
\]

In fact, for \(d\ge2\), the same assertion holds for every compactly supported, non-atomic, centered \(1/d\)-concave probability measure on the line. The original convex-body marginal is such a measure by Brunn–Minkowski. Its density is \(1/(d-1)\)-concave; these two parameters must not be confused.

For \(d=1\), the body is an interval and the two tails sum to one, including all support-endpoint cases. For an actual convex-body marginal, the case \(s=0\) is the ordinary continuous Grünbaum inequality. For the more general non-atomic scalar law, the zero-shift case follows by letting \(s\downarrow0\) after proving the positive-shift assertion. The rest of the proof treats \(d\ge2\) and \(s>0\).

## 2. The exact localization step

We use Theorem 2 of Fradelizi–Guédon, *The Extreme Points of Subsets of s-Concave Probabilities and a Geometric Localization Theorem*, Discrete & Computational Geometry 31 (2004), 327–335, DOI 10.1007/s00454-003-2868-y. [Author-hosted paper](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/fradelizi.matthieu/pdf/localizationDCG.pdf); [author-uploaded full text](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220452814_The_Extreme_Points_of_Subsets_of_s_-Concave_Probabilities_and_a_Geometric_Localization_Theorem).

The needed form is: on a fixed compact convex set, for concavity parameter \(\sigma\le1/2\), a convex upper-semicontinuous functional on \(\sigma\)-concave probabilities subject to one upper-semicontinuous integral constraint attains its supremum at either an admissible Dirac measure or a \(\sigma\)-affine segment probability saturating that constraint.

Fix a compact interval containing the marginal support and impose only

\[
                         \int x\,d\nu(x)\ge0.
\]

Take \(\sigma=1/d\le1/2\), and the affine functional

\[
 \Phi_s(\nu)=\nu(( -\infty,-s])+\nu(( -\infty,s]).             \tag{2}
\]

Both sets are closed relative to the fixed compact interval, so Portmanteau makes (2) upper semicontinuous. The constraint function \(x\) is continuous. The original centered marginal is admissible. An admissible Dirac measure is at a point \(x\ge0\), and its value in (2) is at most one because \(s>0\).

Every non-Dirac extremizer has mean exactly zero and a density proportional to a nonnegative affine function raised to power

\[
                  \frac{1-\sigma}{\sigma}=d-1
\]

on a compact interval. The theorem's additional one-sided moment condition is automatic for a nondegenerate centered interval law: every proper initial integral \(\int_a^x t\,d\nu(t)\) is negative, equivalently every proper final integral is positive. We need only the stated necessary form of the extremizer.

It therefore suffices to prove

\[
                    \Phi_s(\nu)\le2-2\gamma_d               \tag{3}
\]

for these centered affine-power densities. The harmless Dirac values satisfy (3), since \(\gamma_d\le1/2\). The original marginal has no atoms, so (3) translates exactly into (1). No two-equality-constraint localization is used.

## 3. All shifts of an affine-power density

A nonconstant increasing affine-power density can be transformed by an increasing affine change of variable to

\[
  f_{d,r}(t)=\frac{d\,t^{d-1}}{1-r^d}\,\mathbf 1_{[r,1]}(t),
  \qquad 0\le r<1.
\]

Its mean is

\[
 m=\frac d{d+1}\frac{1-r^{d+1}}{1-r^d},
 \qquad \frac{1+r}{2}\le m<1.                              \tag{4}
\]

The first inequality follows by pairing equidistant points about the interval midpoint in the integral of \((t-(1+r)/2)t^{d-1}\). Let \(G\) be this law's CDF and define

\[
                       H(h)=G(m-h)+G(m+h),\qquad h\ge0.
\]

For \(0\le h\le1-m\), both arguments lie in the support and
\(H'(h)=f_{d,r}(m+h)-f_{d,r}(m-h)\ge0\). For
\(1-m\le h\le m-r\), the upper argument is beyond the support, and \(H\) is nonincreasing. Afterwards \(H=1\). Consequently

\[
 \max_{h\ge0}H(h)=1+T_d(r),\qquad
 T_d(r)=\frac{(2m-1)^d-r^d}{1-r^d},                        \tag{5}
\]

and the maximum is attained at \(h=1-m\). Also

\[
                  \min_{h\ge0}H(h)=\min\{2G(m),1\}.         \tag{6}
\]

The decreasing affine-power case is the reflection of this law. Its paired CDF is \(2-H(h)\). The usual continuous Grünbaum theorem gives \(G(m)\ge\gamma_d\): the density in (4) is the first-coordinate marginal of the actual convex frustum
\(\{(t,y):r\le t\le1,\ y\in tL\}\), with any fixed \((d-1)\)-dimensional convex body \(L\). Thus (6) proves (3) for decreasing affine-power densities. Constant affine densities are centered uniform interval laws and have paired CDF identically one.

It remains only to show

\[
                        T_d(r)\le1-2\gamma_d.               \tag{7}
\]

## 4. Exact dimensions two and three

For \(d=2\), direct simplification gives

\[
 T_2(r)=\frac19-\frac{8r^3}{9(1+r)^3}\le\frac19
                  =1-2\gamma_2.                            \tag{8}
\]

For \(d=3\), put \(A=1+r+r^2\) and \(N=A+3r^3\), so
\(2m-1=N/(2A)\). The desired bound \(T_3\le5/32\) is equivalent to

\[
 (5+27r^3)A^3-4N^3\ge0.
\]

Its exact factorization is

\[
 (1-r)(1+4r+10r^2+8r^3+23r^4+80r^5
                  +90r^6+108r^7+81r^8)\ge0.                \tag{9}
\]

This proves (7) in dimension three, including \(r=0\). The excluded parameter \(r=1\) is the degenerate interval limit, where \(T_d\to0\).

## 5. A quadrature inequality

For every \(0<\alpha<1\), \(0\le R<1\), and \(a=(1+5R)/6\),

\[
       \frac2{1-R}\int_R^1 u^\alpha\,du\le1+a^\alpha.        \tag{10}
\]

First prove, for \(0<v\le1\),

\[
 -\log v\ge\frac{(1-v)(7+5v)}{2(1+5v)}.                    \tag{11}
\]

The derivative of the left side minus the right side is

\[
           \frac{(v-1)(5v-1)(5v-2)}{2v(1+5v)^2}.
\]

The only possible minima are at \(v=1\), with value zero, and at \(v=1/5\), with value \(\log5-8/5>0\); the function diverges to infinity at zero. The latter strict inequality has an exact elementary certificate from

\[
 \log5=2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(2/3)^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
 >2\sum_{j=0}^{3}\frac{(2/3)^{2j+1}}{2j+1}>\frac85.
\]

For \(t>0\), set \(v=(R+t)/(1+t)\). Inequality (11) is exactly

\[
 \frac1{1+t}+\frac1{a+t}
 \le\frac2{1-R}\int_R^1\frac{du}{u+t}.                     \tag{12}
\]

For \(0<\alpha<1\), the positive integral representation

\[
 u^\alpha=C_\alpha\int_0^\infty
                t^{\alpha-1}\frac{u}{u+t}\,dt,
 \qquad
 C_\alpha=\left(\int_0^\infty\frac{v^{\alpha-1}}{1+v}\,dv\right)^{-1}>0
\]

follows by scaling; it also holds at \(u=0\). For each \(t>0\), (12) says precisely that

\[
 \frac1{1+t}+\frac a{a+t}
       -\frac2{1-R}\int_R^1\frac u{u+t}\,du\ge0.
\]

Multiplying by \(C_\alpha t^{\alpha-1}\) and integrating proves (10). Every individual integral is finite, so this step does not subtract divergent quantities.

## 6. All higher dimensions

In (10), take \(\alpha=1/d\) and \(R=r^d\). Formula (4) says

\[
                 m=\frac1{1-R}\int_R^1u^{1/d}\,du.
\]

Thus \(2m-1\le((1+5R)/6)^{1/d}\). The left side is nonnegative by (4), so

\[
       T_d(r)\le\frac{(1+5R)/6-R}{1-R}=\frac16.              \tag{13}
\]

For \(d\ge4\), \(\gamma_d\le\gamma_4=256/625\), and

\[
              1-2\gamma_4=\frac{113}{625}>\frac16.
\]

Monotonicity of \(\gamma_d\) follows from differentiating
\(-d\log(1+1/d)\) and using \(\log(1+x)>x/(1+x)\). Therefore (13) proves (7) for all remaining dimensions. Together with localization this completes (1).

## 7. Independent symmetric additive noise

Let \(X\) be uniform on \(K\), and let \(Y\) be independent of \(X\), with a distribution symmetric about zero. Then every closed halfspace through \(g\) has

\[
                         \mathbb P(X+Y\in H)\ge\gamma_d.    \tag{14}
\]

Indeed, in the halfspace's scalar normal direction, the law of \(u\cdot Y\) is symmetric. Pair its values \(s,-s\) and use (1); its mass at zero uses the ordinary centroid bound. This argument does not require a density for the noise. If the noise has a finite first moment, \(g\) is also the convolution centroid. The constant is sharp by zero noise and a simplex.

Consequently, for an actual product body \(C=P\times K\), where \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) is centrally symmetric about an integer point \(j\), the mixed-volume centroid \((j,g)\) has normalized mixed halfspace depth at least \(\gamma_d\). The finite uniform law on \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\) is symmetric about \(j\); every oblique ambient halfspace becomes (14) after conditioning on the base. Vertical halfspaces through \(j\) have mass at least one half. Also \(j\in P\), so the center is an actual mixed point. No analogous conclusion for non-product compatible fibers is asserted.

## 8. Screens, equality cautions, and scope

Before the proof, exact rational screens tested 60,000 piecewise-linear concave planar profiles and 20,000 piecewise-affine concave-root profiles in each of dimensions 3, 4, 5, 8, 12, and 20. They found no violations. Their scripts are `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/screen_paired_concave_tails.py` and `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/screen_paired_power_tails.py`; they are evidence only and are not used in this proof.

The minimum paired-tail sum need not occur at zero shift. For the increasing triangular density on \([0,1]\), mean \(2/3\), shift \(1/3\) gives paired tails \(8/9\), while their sum at zero is \(10/9\). Also \(T_d(r)\) is not generally monotone in \(r\) for \(d\ge3\); no cone-only extremizer assertion is used.

The exact verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_paired_centroid_tail_scalar_certificates.py` checks (8), (9), the rational derivative numerator in (11), the four-term logarithm certificate, and the dimension-four comparison. The external dependency is only the explicitly cited localization theorem and the ordinary continuous Grünbaum inequality.
